newsitem.title: USA: US stocks end lower as late selling staggers techs.
newsitem.headline: US stocks end lower as late selling staggers techs.

text.p: U.S. stocks closed lower as a wave of profit-taking among technology stocks snowballed in the aftermath of a computer retailer's disappointing earnings.
The Dow industrials fell 37 points to close unofficially at 6268. The tech-laden Nasdaq Composite closed at 1261, down 24 points. The decline was Nasdaq's steepest since July 23.
"The carnage today begins and ends with technology," said Philip Orlando, chief investment officer at Value Line Asset Management.
Some of the session's steepest losses were posted by the top technology names, which analysts saw as a sign investors had decided to realize some of their profits.
"If you're going to take profits in this market, the large-cap techs would clearly be the obvious targets," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany.

Analysts also cited weak results from electronics retailer Circuit City Stores Inc where fiscal third quarter earnings fell to $0.20 per share from $0.32 a year ago. The company cited soft personal computer sales for the decline.

"During the third quarter, sales of personal computers weakened dramatically while sales of most consumer electronic products remained soft," Circuit City chairman and chief executive said Richard Sharp said in a statement.
Analysts said the already apprehensive market seized on the news and took the opportunity to sell.

"The market is assuming that because one bad retailer reported sloppy earnings, the entire tech industry is going to hell in a handbasket," said Orlando. "Technology investors tend to be very nervous and in this case the response was overblown."

The broad selling pressure hit hardest among the largest technology names. Shares in International Business Machines Corp fell 4-1/8 to 148-3/4 and Intel Corp fell 5-1/8 to 127-1/4. Microsoft Corp fell 3-1/4 to 76-3/4.
Heightened caution was also evident when investment firm Morgan Stanley's global strategist Barton Biggs recommended shifting some funds out of stocks into cash and bonds.

The move altered Morgan Stanley's global asset allocation portfolio to 56 percent stocks, 29 percent bonds and 15 percent cash. The portfolio had been weighted 74 percent to stocks and 26 percent to bonds before the switch.

The sequence of bad news for stocks overshadowed the announcement that Boeing Co would acquire McDonnell Douglas Corp for more than $13 billion in stock. Shares in both companies soared on the deal, with Boeing up four to 100-3/4 and McDonnell Douglas jumping 10-1/2 to 62-1/2.

The major oil companies provided one of the few other pockets of strength, as forecasts of cold winter weather pushed crude prices sharply higher. Texaco Inc rose 1/2 to 96-3/4 and Chevron Corp gained 1-1/8 to 63-1/8.
Analysts said the mood on Wall Street would likely remain cautious at least until markets received word of the outcome of tomorrow's meeting of the Federal Reserve's Open Market Committee (FOMC).
Release of stronger than expected industrial production data early today depressed the bond market all session, a response analysts attributed to the proximity of the meeting.

"The Fed doesn't set policy decisions on one number but the fact that it's the day before the meeting has people nervous," said Robert Froehlich, chief investment strategist at Van Kampen American Capital.

The FOMC meeting, always closely watched, will likely draw broader attention because of the recent speech by Fed chairman Alan Greenspan, whose passing rhetorical reference to "irrational exuberance" still rings in Wall Street's ears.
NYSE declining issues led advancers by a roughly two-to-one margin.
The Nasdaq Composite fell 23.93 to 1260.98.
The S&P 500 fell 7.65 to 720.99.
(Figures official as of 1645 EST/2145 GMT).
